The god in my kettle was no bigger than a thumbprint and had, he told me, been worshipped inconsistently.

I found him while descaling. He was sitting behind the heating element with his arms crossed, wearing a crown made from a twist tie and an expression of profound administrative disappointment.

“You’re a god?” I said.

“Obviously.”

“Of what?”

He gestured at the kettle. “This. Mostly.”

Later, after I had apologized and offered him the saucer from my best cup, he explained that he had once been a god of thresholds: doorways, dawn, the moment before an answer. Boiling water was one of his smaller parishes. People used to pray to him without knowing it. They stood in kitchens at night, waiting for the kettle, and for three or four minutes they wanted nothing except what they already had.

“Now you scroll,” he said.

For releasing him from the limescale, he offered me one wish. He warned me that his powers had contracted.

“I can make the bus arrive as you reach the stop. I can return one sock from the country of socks. I can ensure that a penny you find is facing the correct way.”

“Can you make Mara come back?”

He looked at me with the tired patience of someone whose worshippers always asked for weather when offered a candle.

“She has a will,” he said. “I have a heating element.”

So I kept the wish.

He stayed for a while. He slept in the sugar bowl and complained about the quality of my tea. Occasionally he performed small kindnesses. The radio played a song I needed without knowing why. My neighbor’s baby slept through the night. A letter I had been afraid to open turned out to contain nothing frightening, only a form, and even gods, he said, must sometimes contend with forms.

At night we talked.

Mara had left in October. I had preserved the apartment in a way that must have been exhausting for the apartment. Her cup remained by the sink. Her book remained facedown on the arm of the sofa, holding its place in a chapter she would never finish here. I had become very skilled at standing in doorways after people had gone.

“What do gods wish for?” I asked him one evening.

He was watching rain stipple the window.

“I have been steam,” he said, “but I have never been weather.”

The next morning, I put him in my coat pocket and took him to the sea.

The journey involved two trains, one bus that arrived suspiciously promptly, and a long argument with a ticket machine. He spent most of it silent. When we finally reached the coast, the wind was cold enough to make my eyes water, and the sea was the color of old cutlery.

I lifted him onto the palm of my hand.

For a long time he said nothing. Waves arrived, considered the shore, and withdrew. Gulls hung above us as if pinned to the gray sky.

“No lid,” he whispered.

Then he laughed.

It began as a small sound, hardly more than a kettle thinking about boiling. It grew until I had to hold him with both hands. Somewhere beyond the headland, thunder answered.

He stepped down onto the sand. He did not grow larger, but he seemed to occupy more of the world.

“About that wish,” he said.

“I wish to stop waiting in rooms people have left.”

He nodded.

“That I can help with,” he said. “Not do. Help with.”

He touched my finger. There was a small, ordinary warmth, the kind by which a hand knows it is holding a cup.

Then he walked into the spray.

I waited until evening, but he did not come back. Once, far offshore, I thought I saw a white cloud no bigger than a thumbprint, racing the other clouds and winning.

At home, I washed Mara’s cup. I closed her book and put it on the shelf. I opened the windows, though it was cold, and let the rooms practice being rooms again.

Then I made tea.

I drank it while it was hot. When the telephone rang, I answered it. When it didn’t, I went for a walk. These were not triumphs. No music played. But gradually the future stopped resembling a corridor at the end of which someone might return, and became instead a field: inconveniently open, full of weather.

Sometimes, on clear nights, I wonder whether he remembers me. Probably gods have more important things to remember. Oceans. Dawns. The names of doors.

Still, every kettle since then has sounded to me like the sea practicing.
